items.title: Basics are boring, but they save lives in interviews
items.author: Suraj Khonde
items.description:
👦 Nephew: Uncle, you look upset. Was the interview really that tough?
👨‍🦳 Uncle: Tough? No… that’s the worst part. It wasn’t tough at all. They just asked me to write a simple callback, a Promise, and async/await.
👦 Nephew:That’s all? But you know those things!
👨‍🦳 Uncle:I know them, yes. But when I had to actually type the syntax without VS Code helping me… my brain just went blank.
👦 Nephew:Ohh… like when you think you know a song but when the mic comes in your hand you forget the lyrics?
👨‍🦳 Uncle: Exactly! Perfect example. I know the definitions, I can explain them, but when it came to writing, I froze and messed up.
👦 Nephew:But uncle, how can someone with three years’ experience fail at basics?
👨‍🦳 Uncle:Because I kept chasing advanced topics. I read about caching, load balancers, performance tricks… but I stopped practicing the very basics.
👦 Nephew:So basics are more important than advanced things?
👨‍🦳 Uncle: Basics are the foundation. You can decorate the house with fancy stuff, but if the foundation is weak, the whole thing collapses. That’s what happened to me.

👨‍🦳 Uncle: Listen, don’t stand like a deer staring at water in the desert when interview time comes. Go back to basics. Make your hands dirty on pen and paper or a plain online compiler. Avoid copy–paste. At work, yes, we use tools, autocomplete, snippets — that’s fine. But in interviews, only muscle memory saves you. Nobody cares if VS Code closes your brackets. They want to see if you can write it. Practice raw, simple, and real. That’s the only way to build confidence.

👨‍🦳 Uncle: And one more thing — don’t get distracted by fancy YouTube videos where people talk about system design, rate limiters, or reverse proxies. Those things matter later, but if you’re like me — a small developer starting your career and targeting a decent, well-paid job — then focus on the basics of your tech stack first. That’s what really gets you hired.

👦 Nephew:Hmm… so what’s the plan now?
👨‍🦳 Uncle:From now on, I’ll practice the small things every single day. Not just theory — I’ll actually write callbacks, promises, async/await, arrays, strings… all of it.
👦 Nephew:On VS Code?
Uncle: No, no. On a plain editor. No shortcuts, no autocomplete. Even React basics — I’ll type the syntax myself, like old-school days. No fast code-writing tools. Just me, my hands, and the keyboard. That’s the only way to build real muscle memory.

items.title: seven ways to secure your Node.js
items.author: Suraj Khonde
items.description:
seven ways to secure your Node.js.

These are practical tips you can apply right away. I’ll keep the code examples simple and the language even simpler. Let’s get into it.

1. Use Environment Variables

Storing sensitive data like database credentials, API keys, or JWT secrets directly in your code is risky. If your code ends up in the wrong hands, so does everything else.

Instead, store this data in a .env file and use the dotenv package to access it:

require('dotenv').config();
const dbPassword = process.env.DB_PASSWORD;

Make sure you never commit your .env file. Add it to your .gitignore file to keep it private.

2. Validate All Input

Attackers love user input.

If you don’t check what comes into your API, they’ll sneak in commands, inject code, or crash your app.

The best way to stop them is by validating every piece of input. Use a package like Joi or zod to define what your API expects:

const Joi = require('joi');

const schema = Joi.object({
  username: Joi.string().alphanum().min(3).max(30).required(),
  password: Joi.string().pattern(new RegExp('^[a-zA-Z0-9]{6,30}$')).required()
});
const { error } = schema.validate(req.body);
if (error) {
  return res.status(400).send(error.details[0].message);
}

In the above code, we have defined the exact data type the schema expects. This way, wrong data gets blocked before it reaches your logic or database.

3. Rate Limit Your Endpoints

Bots and brute force attacks work by flooding your server with requests. Once your server reaches it limit, your API will crash.

Set a limit on how often a user can hit your API using middleware like express-rate-limit Here is an example.

const rateLimit = require('express-rate-limit');

const limiter = rateLimit({
  windowMs: 15 * 60 * 1000, // 15 minutes
  max: 100 // limit each IP to 100 requests per windowMs
});
app.use('/api/', limiter);

The above code restricts API requests coming from an IP address to 100 per 15 minutes. This is like putting a speed bump in front of a runaway car.

4. Always Use HTTPS

HTTP sends data in plain text. That means anyone between your server and the user can read it. HTTPS encrypts everything. It’s not optional anymore.

If you’re using a platform like Heroku or Vercel, HTTPS is automatic. If you’re self-hosting, you can set it up with services like Let’s Encrypt.

Also, force HTTPS on all incoming traffic. You can use middleware like this:

app.use((req, res, next) => {
  if (req.headers['x-forwarded-proto'] !== 'https') {
    return res.redirect('https://' + req.headers.host + req.url);
  }
  next();
});

Encrypt the ride. Always.

5. Use Helmet to Secure HTTP Headers

HTTP headers are key-value pairs sent in requests and responses over the web. They give extra information about what’s being sent – like who’s sending it, what type it is, how it should be handled, and more.

HTTP headers are small, but they can be powerful tools to protect your app. Helmet is a Node.js middleware that sets secure headers for you.

const helmet = require('helmet');
app.use(helmet());

Helmet helps prevent attacks like cross-site scripting (XSS), clickjacking, and others just by setting the right headers.

One line of code, a big step up in security.

6. Sanitize Data to Prevent Injection Attacks

Injection attacks happen when you blindly trust input and plug it into a command or query.

For example, an attacker might submit a piece of text that turns into a command in your database.

You should sanitize data before it gets to any sensitive function. Libraries like express-mongo-sanitize or xss-clean help clean up malicious input.

const mongoSanitize = require('express-mongo-sanitize');
const xss = require('xss-clean');

app.use(mongoSanitize());
app.use(xss());

This strips out dangerous characters and scripts that could do real damage.

7. Use Strong Authentication and Authorisation

Authentication is about knowing who the user is, and authorisation is about what they can do. You need both, and you need them to be strong.

Use JWT (JSON Web Tokens) or sessions to manage logged-in users. Here’s a quick JWT example:

const jwt = require('jsonwebtoken');

const token = jwt.sign({ id: user._id }, process.env.JWT_SECRET, {
  expiresIn: '1h'
});
const decoded = jwt.verify(token, process.env.JWT_SECRET);

And don’t forget roles. A user who can view data shouldn’t be able to delete it unless they’re supposed to.

Security isn’t just a feature – it’s a habit. You can’t do everything all at once, but you can start with a few key changes.

Use environment variables. Validate your inputs. Add rate limiting. Move to HTTPS. Install Helmet. Sanitize everything. Lock down your authentication.

Each of these steps is a small lock on a big door. The more you add, the harder it is for someone to break in. So take a little time now. Your future self and your users will thank you.

items.title: What Happens When You Click a Button? ️
items.author: Suraj Khonde
items.description:
(How data flows from your browser to the server and back)

👦 Nephew:Uncle, when I click a button on a website and data comes, what magic is happening behind the scenes?

👨‍🦳 Uncle:Haha, son, it’s not magic. It’s a whole system working together. Let me explain like an eagle flying high 🦅, seeing the big picture.

When you click that button, your browser prepares a request. Think of it like writing a postcard to someone you care about:

  • You write the address (URL → domain + path).
  • You write your message (payload), like sending text, images, or video.
  • You add some extra info, like whether the address is protected and needs authorization.

There are two common ways to prove you are allowed to send this request:
1. Using JWT token

const payload = { title: 'Hello', body: 'World' };

fetch('https://api.example.com/posts', {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: {
    'Content-Type': 'application/json',     // tells server we send JSON
    'Accept': 'application/json',
    'Authorization': 'Bearer eyJhbGciOi...' // JWT token
  },
  body: JSON.stringify(payload)
})
  .then(res => res.json())
  .then(data => console.log(data));

2. Using Cookies

Browsers send cookies automatically for same-site requests. For cross-site or explicit sending:

fetch('https://api.example.com/user/profile', {
  method: 'GET',
  credentials: 'include'   // 'same-origin' or 'include' to send cookies
})
  .then(res => res.json())
  .then(profile => console.log(profile));

👨‍🦳 Uncle:But son, your browser does one more thing than a normal postcard. It sends a preflight request to the server first, asking: ‘Can I talk to you?’

If the server says yes, only then your actual request is sent.

👦 Nephew:Uncle, it’s a bit confusing. How does the server know who to talk to and who not?

Uncle:Think of a door that’s open for everyone. Sometimes unwanted guests come, the server gets busy, and real guests have to wait. So we add an initial layer called CORS to check who is allowed.

👦 Nephew:Ah, that’s why sometimes I see CORS errors! Can you explain what it means?

Uncle:Sure! CORS stands for Cross-Origin Resource Sharing.

Think like this:

  • You are at your own house (domain A).
  • You want to borrow sugar from your neighbor (domain B).
  • Before entering, you must ask: ‘Hey, can I come in?’

This asking is the preflight request (OPTIONS). The browser automatically checks:

  • Is this API endpoint open for me?
  • Does the server allow my origin (my website) to access it?
  • Which methods are allowed (GET, POST, PUT)?
  • Are special headers allowed (Authorization, Content-Type: application/json)?

If the server replies ✅ yes → your main request is sent.
If the server replies ❌ no → your request is blocked before it even leaves.

const express = require('express');
const cors = require('cors');
const app = express();

// Basic setup: allow one origin
app.use(cors({
  origin: 'http://localhost:3000',
  methods: ['GET', 'POST', 'PUT', 'DELETE'],
  allowedHeaders: ['Content-Type', 'Authorization'],
  credentials: true // allow cookies if needed
}));

Uncle:So, CORS is like a security guard at the gate. It doesn’t care how powerful you are inside, it just checks whether you are allowed in. 🚪

👦 Nephew:Ohhh… so preflight is like a guard’s ID check before I enter?

👨‍🦳 Uncle:Exactly, son. Without this, any random website could steal your cookies and data.
👦 Nephew:So after the browser packs the envelope, where does it go?

👨‍🦳 Uncle:Ahh, now the journey begins! Think of it like a car traveling on highways to reach another city. 🚗

Your request doesn’t teleport. It passes through different layers:

  • DNS 📖 → Like a phonebook. You ask: ‘What’s the number (IP) of example.com?’
  • TCP/IP 📦 → Ensures the letter travels safely, piece by piece, like breaking a big box into parcels.
  • HTTP/HTTPS 📨 → Language of the web. HTTPS encrypts it 🔒.
Browser (You)
   |
   |  (DNS: find address)
   v
IP Address (Server's house)
   |
   |  (TCP/IP: safe delivery)
   v
HTTP/HTTPS (actual message)
   |
   v
Server (Destination)

👦 Nephew:So, DNS finds the house, TCP/IP carries the parcels safely, and HTTP/HTTPS is the language of the letter?

👨‍🦳 Uncle:Yes, son. Without these highways, your request would get lost. 🌌

👦 Nephew:Uncle, why do we need JWT tokens? I already know the server’s address. If I know the class, can’t I just go sit there?

👨‍🦳 Uncle:Son, in your school, you also know where the computer class and chemistry lab are. So why don’t you just walk in?

👦 Nephew(smiling):Haha 🤣, I’ll attend higher classes, play in labs, and maybe sneak into the teacher’s room.

👨‍🦳 Uncle:That’s where the ID card comes in. Your ID card tells:

  • Who you are 🧑 (Authentication)
  • What you’re allowed to access 🎫 (Authorization)

Imagine — you’re just a small teacher’s assistant. Last time you mistakenly deleted some computer data 💻❌, so now you’re not authorized to sit in the computer class. Chemistry labs? Too dangerous ☠️, you’re not allowed there either.

👨‍🦳 Uncle: Same in servers:

  • JWT = your school ID card
  • Authentication = proves who you are
  • Authorization = defines which classes you can enter

Without these checks, requests could mess up other parts of the system. Every request must carry its ID card (token) before entering.
👦 Nephew(thinking):That’s why the gatekeeper always asks for my ID card. But uncle, how does the server remember my password even after a week?

👨‍🦳 Uncle:Son, the server is like a cook 👨‍🍳. He doesn’t remember everything. He takes your order, prepares the dish 🍲, and stores all important info in the database.

When you log in, the server cross-checks your details. If correct ✅, it issues you an ID card (JWT) containing:

  • 🆔 User ID
  • 👤 Name
  • 🎭 Role (student, teacher, admin)

Next time you visit, you just show your ID card. JWT acts like a security guard 👮 who checks your card and lets you in without asking your password every time.

👦 Nephew(wide-eyed):Wow uncle! Now I’ll never forget. One is like a temporary leave pass, and the other is like an ID card I carry — but even that has an expiry, like one year or whatever the server decides.

👨‍🦳 Uncle(smiling):Exactly, son! JWTs are like ID cards that prove who you are, but they can expire. Once expired, you need to get a new one. That way, old tokens don’t stay valid forever — it keeps the system safe.

👨‍🦳 Uncle:Now, the server has passed your request through middleware. It goes to the database (library) to find the right book (data).

  • Server does only light CPU work (math, arranging info)
  • Database (librarian) finds the exact record 📖
  • Formats it as HTML 📝, JSON 📦, or streams video 🎥

Status codes tell you:

  • ✅ 200 OK → Here’s your book!
  • ⚠️ 404 Not Found → No such book
  • ⛔ 403 Forbidden → Not allowed
  • 💥 500 Server Error → Something broke

Status codes are like short report cards 🗒️ for your request.

👨‍🦳 Uncle:The server packs everything in a response envelope:

  • Data → JSON, HTML, video
  • Headers → Status code, cache-control, cookies

Then it travels back through the same network highways 🌐 (HTTP → TCP/IP → DNS).

Finally, it lands safely in your browser 🖥️. The browser opens it and paints the UI 🎨.

A message from our Founder

Hey, Sunil here. I wanted to take a moment to thank you for reading until the end and for being a part of this community.

Did you know that our team run these publications as a volunteer effort to over 3.5m monthly readers? We don’t receive any funding, we do this to support the community. ❤️

If you want to show some love, please take a moment to follow me on LinkedIn, TikTok, Instagram. You can also subscribe to our weekly newsletter.

And before you go, don’t forget to clap and follow the writer️!

  • HTTP/HTTPS 📨 → Language of the web. HTTPS encrypts it 🔒.
Browser (You)
   |
   |  (DNS: find address)
   v
IP Address (Server's house)
   |
   |  (TCP/IP: safe delivery)
   v
HTTP/HTTPS (actual message)
   |
   v
Server (Destination)

👦 Nephew:So, DNS finds the house, TCP/IP carries the parcels safely, and HTTP/HTTPS is the language of the letter?

👨‍🦳 Uncle:Yes, son. Without these highways, your request would get lost. 🌌

👦 Nephew:Uncle, why do we need JWT tokens? I already know the server’s address. If I know the class, can’t I just go sit there?

👨‍🦳 Uncle:Son, in your school, you also know where the computer class and chemistry lab are. So why don’t you just walk in?

👦 Nephew(smiling):Haha 🤣, I’ll attend higher classes, play in labs, and maybe sneak into the teacher’s room.

👨‍🦳 Uncle:That’s where the ID card comes in. Your ID card tells:

  • Who you are 🧑 (Authentication)
  • What you’re allowed to access 🎫 (Authorization)

Imagine — you’re just a small teacher’s assistant. Last time you mistakenly deleted some computer data 💻❌, so now you’re not authorized to sit in the computer class. Chemistry labs? Too dangerous ☠️, you’re not allowed there either.

👨‍🦳 Uncle: Same in servers:

  • JWT = your school ID card
  • Authentication = proves who you are
  • Authorization = defines which classes you can enter

Without these checks, requests could mess up other parts of the system. Every request must carry its ID card (token) before entering.
👦 Nephew(thinking):That’s why the gatekeeper always asks for my ID card. But uncle, how does the server remember my password even after a week?

👨‍🦳 Uncle:Son, the server is like a cook 👨‍🍳. He doesn’t remember everything. He takes your order, prepares the dish 🍲, and stores all important info in the database.

When you log in, the server cross-checks your details. If correct ✅, it issues you an ID card (JWT) containing:

  • 🆔 User ID
  • 👤 Name
  • 🎭 Role (student, teacher, admin)

Next time you visit, you just show your ID card. JWT acts like a security guard 👮 who checks your card and lets you in without asking your password every time.

👦 Nephew(wide-eyed):Wow uncle! Now I’ll never forget. One is like a temporary leave pass, and the other is like an ID card I carry — but even that has an expiry, like one year or whatever the server decides.

👨‍🦳 Uncle(smiling):Exactly, son! JWTs are like ID cards that prove who you are, but they can expire. Once expired, you need to get a new one. That way, old tokens don’t stay valid forever — it keeps the system safe.

  • Server does only light CPU work (math, arranging info)
  • Database (librarian) finds the exact record 📖
  • Formats it as HTML 📝, JSON 📦, or streams video 🎥

Status codes tell you:

  • ✅ 200 OK → Here’s your book!
  • ⚠️ 404 Not Found → No such book
  • ⛔ 403 Forbidden → Not allowed
  • 💥 500 Server Error → Something broke

Status codes are like short report cards 🗒️ for your request.

👨‍🦳 Uncle:The server packs everything in a response envelope:

  • Data → JSON, HTML, video
  • Headers → Status code, cache-control, cookies

Then it travels back through the same network highways 🌐 (HTTP → TCP/IP → DNS).

Finally, it lands safely in your browser 🖥️. The browser opens it and paints the UI 🎨.

items.title: Why Being a Good Developer Isn’t Enough — Think Like an Engineer
items.author: Suraj Khonde
items.description:
Why Being a Good Developer Isn’t Enough — Think Like an Engineer

👦 Nephew: Uncle, all this React you taught me… if you teach me Node.js too, will that make me a good developer or an engineer?

👨‍🦳 Uncle: Haha, yes! It will make you a good React and Node.js developer, not necessarily an engineer.

👦 Nephew:Oh… (sad tone) Uncle, how do I become a good engineer? Do I need an engineering degree?

👨‍🦳 Uncle: No, no child, calm down. Engineering is a thought process and a systematic way to approach problems. In development, the problems are usually business problems.

👦 Nephew:What do you mean by system?

👨‍🦳 Uncle: Look, writing code is just one piece of our puzzle. There are several pieces that need to be there to make the whole picture.

👦 Nephew:Wow, it’s getting interesting! Can you just shed some light on it?

👨‍🦳 Uncle: Okay, until now you’ve been working on some projects or problems, so we can move a step ahead.
Look, son, why do we use React when we have plain JavaScript which browsers can understand easily?

👦 Nephew: Aha… (thinking)
React solves the problem by developing the UI in smaller pieces, making it easier to maintain, develop, and reuse. It’s also easier to handle data using props, useContext, events, Redux, and it only re-renders what’s necessary for fast UI.

👨‍🦳 Uncle: Wow! Look, React solves so many problems. Now think — when you built a house in your childhood, how did you approach that building process?

👦 Nephew: I built walls, made the roof, created small rooms, painted it, and made sure all rooms had light, water, and other necessary things.

👨‍🦳 Uncle:Same! When you build a home, you follow a system. It’s the same with apps.
You make a clear design: how you will build the application, create folder structure, choose the right tech stack for the current situation, and make a clear folder structure.

👦 Nephew: Yes, uncle! That is very important. I learned through this mistake — I used the server API URL in the entire project, and when I needed to replace the dev API, I forgot where I used it. I didn’t track it.

👨‍🦳 Uncle: Hey, don’t worry. That small mistake is practice. It will make things less painful in real projects.
So yes, always make sure all APIs are in one place, dynamically, in an api folder. Basically, here is the folder structure…

src/
├── assets/       
├── components/    
├── context/   here Api can save  
├── hooks/        
├── pages/        
├── services/     
├── store/        
├── utils/        
└── App.jsx

👨‍🦳 Uncle: Now think like an engineer. Here are some rules I will give you today:

  1. Always develop apps from the user’s point of view. Make it easy to use without conscious thought.
    👉 Example: scroll up → next video, scroll down → previous video. Users don’t need to think twice or remember steps.
  2. Always use simple logic. Don’t overcomplicate. If you must use complexity, leave comments. When you write code, you understand it now, but in the future, you’ll forget the context.
  3. Don’t over-engineer: small unnecessary components don’t need to be wrapped in React.memo or small computed code in useMemo.
  4. If you are developing both client and server, still don’t trust blindly. As a frontend developer, don’t trust server API responses — make sure the app doesn’t crash on type errors. As a backend developer, don’t trust what the frontend sends — always cross-check input fields.
  5. Before shutting down or closing the day, always push the code to Git. Never be lazy. If the main branch is busy, create another branch, but always push.
  6. Engineering is about efficiency: avoid unnecessary re-renders or repetition on both server and client.
  7. Technology will always evolve. Don’t get stuck in hours of learning. Ask why this tech exists, what problem it solves, how it works, and where you can implement it. Learn the basics, then get your hands dirty.
  8. Most important: always remember — eat the elephant piece by piece 🐘.
  9. Error handling is essential: Often we think “I know what I’m doing,” so we overlook errors. But small mistakes, when they become part of a bigger system, can turn into real problems later. Catch them early — it saves huge pain down the road.
  10. Centralize configs: Don’t scatter API endpoints, constants, or environment variables all over your project. Keep them in one place. This way, when something changes, you don’t have to hunt everywhere — it saves time and avoids chaos.
  11. Learn continuously, but practically: Don’t just chase the latest frameworks. Focus on the basics — they pay off the most. For example, JavaScript is 80% of our daily coding. Understanding how things work under the hood — like HTTP, the JS engine, or DB queries — makes you a smarter engineer and helps you solve real problems faster.

You know why the turtle won the race while the talented rabbit lost, even though the rabbit had all the power and speed? 🐢🏁

Because the turtle kept walking, step by step, following a system. Everyone knew the rabbit would win, but the turtle didn’t rush, didn’t panic, and stayed consistent.
The lesson? In development (and in life), talent alone isn’t enough. Systematic thinking, discipline, and steady progress always win the race.

items.title: Newfew Learns Why Redux Exists
items.author: Suraj Khonde
items.description:
👦 Nephew: Uncle, you already explained useContext to me. But my friends keep saying Redux Toolkit is important. Why do we really need Redux? Where does it fit in?

👨‍🦳 Uncle:Look, child. Every system exists to solve a problem. Let me take you back in time.

Your grandfather had a small shop. It only served daily items like milk and bread. Everything was simple. Customers came, asked for something, and got it directly.

👉 This is like useContext — one place (the shop), everyone can access what they need.

👦 Nephew:Yes, like useContext! I get the item directly, update it, and everyone knows.

👨‍🦳 Uncle:Exactly. But as the shop grew, grandfather added vegetables, rice, clothes, snacks — many categories. Now it became a big warehouse (single source of truth ).

Here’s how things worked:

  • Customers (your React components) don’t touch the stock directly.
  • They write a request slip saying what they want.
    Example: { type: "BUY_APPLE", payload: 2 }

👉 That slip is an Action.

But soon, problems appeared:

  • Too many customers rushing in.
  • No proper manager.
  • Anyone could take or add items to the warehouse.
  • Stock got messed up.
  • Some people even cheated with the money 😅.

👦 Nephew: Oh, so if everyone can control the store, it becomes chaos!

👨‍🦳 Uncle: Exactly! That’s when grandfather appointed a Manager.

  • The Manager = Reducer.
  • The Warehouse = Store.

Now the rule is simple:

  1. Customer gives a request slip (Action).
  2. The Manager checks:
  • Current stock (State)
  • The request slip (Action)
  1. Manager updates the warehouse and creates a new stock record (new State).

👉 That’s why Redux is unidirectional:
Customer → Request Slip (Action) → Manager (Reducer) → Warehouse (Store) → Customer

👦 Nephew: Haha, so the manager doesn’t eat apples himself?

👨‍🦳 Uncle:😅 Exactly! The manager never mutates stock directly. He only calculates the next state. That’s why Redux is predictable and traceable.

👦 Nephew: But Uncle, can we have multiple stores?

Uncle:In real life yes, but in Redux we keep one warehouse. Inside it, we organize shelves:

  • Fruits section → userSlice
  • Vegetables section → cartSlice
  • Snacks section → ordersSlice

👉 So, one warehouse (one Redux store), but neatly divided into sections (slices).

Newfew:
Now I get it! UseContext works for small shops. But when my app becomes a big market like Amazon, I need Redux Toolkit to manage things cleanly.

👨‍🦳 Uncle:Hey Newfew, I’ll provide you a small code snippet. This will help you set up a Redux store and slice. Imagine this is your fruit section (Apple stock) in grandfather’s warehouse. 🍎

// store.js
import { configureStore, createSlice } from '@reduxjs/toolkit';

// 1️⃣ Create a slice (like fruit section in warehouse)
const fruitSlice = createSlice({
  name: 'fruit',
  initialState: { apples: 10 },
  reducers: {
    buyApple: (state, action) => {
      state.apples -= action.payload; // customer buys apples
    },
    restockApple: (state, action) => {
      state.apples += action.payload; // new stock added
    }
  }
});

// Export actions
export const { buyApple, restockApple } = fruitSlice.actions;

// 2️⃣ Create a store (the warehouse)
const store = configureStore({
  reducer: {
    fruit: fruitSlice.reducer
  }
});

export default store;

In React App (like customers using apples):

// App.js
import React from 'react';
import { Provider, useSelector, useDispatch } from 'react-redux';
import store, { buyApple, restockApple } from './store';

function FruitShop() {
  const apples = useSelector((state) => state.fruit.apples); // read stock
  const dispatch = useDispatch();

  return (
    <div>
      <h1>🍎 Apples left: {apples}</h1>
      <button onClick={() => dispatch(buyApple(1))}>Buy 1 Apple</button>
      <button onClick={() => dispatch(restockApple(5))}>Restock 5 Apples</button>
    </div>
  );
}

export default function App() {
  return (
    <Provider store={store}>
      <FruitShop />
    </Provider>
  );
}

⚡ Summary for Newfew:

  • useContext = Small shop, easy sharing, no big rules.
  • Redux Toolkit = Big warehouse with Manager, Request slips, Sections → Perfect for large apps with complex state.

items.description:
👦 Nephew:Uncle, my friends keep talking about useContext. But I don’t get it. If we can just pass details from parent to child directly, why do we need all this?

👨‍🦳 Uncle: Nice question! Sit here, sit here. By the way, I heard your mom packed your favorite food in today’s tiffin. Did you taste it?

👦 Nephew:Oh… I didn’t get it.

👨‍🦳 Uncle:What do you mean? Did you forget your tiffin at home?

👦 Nephew:No, Uncle. I took it to school. But when I wanted my friend to taste it, I passed the tiffin across all the desks until it reached him. By the time it reached, it was almost empty, and I didn’t even get it back! Finally, I had to go to the canteen to buy lunch for myself.

Uncle (laughing):Haha! That’s exactly what happens in prop drilling. You’re passing data (your tiffin) through every student (component) in the row, even though they don’t need it. And by the time it reaches your friend (deep component), it’s messy.

👦 Nephew: Ohhh… so that’s the problem.

}

  • ❌ Becomes messy if you create too many contexts.
  • ❌ No built-in tools like debugging, time-travel, or middleware (unlike Redux Toolkit).

items.title: From Callback Hell to Async Heaven
items.author: Suraj Khonde
items.description:
👦 Nephew: Hey uncle, I learned about callbacks today. A function passed to another function as an argument, and it’s called later when the job is done. Cool, right? Like passing the ball in a game!

👨‍🦳 Uncle:Exactly! Callbacks are awesome. Even things like map, filter, and onClick use callbacks. But remember, child — with great power comes… some problems.

👦 Nephew: (confused) Problems? But callbacks work fine!

👨‍🦳 Uncle: Remember last month when you went to the bank? You just wanted to change one signature in your account.

👦 Nephew: (groans) Don’t remind me! First I went to the reception. Then they sent me to the Relationship Manager. Then to the Branch Manager. Then back to another counter… I felt like I was stuck in an infinite loop of counters! No clear path, just frustration.

👨‍🦳 Uncle:That’s exactly what happens in “callback hell.” One callback calls another callback, which calls another… and your code looks like a staircase of pain.

👦 Nephew: (laughs) Yes, I don’t want my code to feel like visiting that bank again.

👨‍🦳 Uncle:That’s why Promises were born. Instead of being tossed from counter to counter, you can make a clear, structured flow.
First .then() → submit form,
Next .then() → manager verifies,
Next .then() → request approved.
Simple, readable, and you always know what’s next.

// Example with Promises
getForm()
  .then(form => submitForm(form))
  .then(response => verifyManager(response))
  .then(approval => console.log("Approved:", approval))
  .catch(error => console.error("Error:", error));

👦 Nephew: Ahhh… so Promises are like a proper queue system. One step after another, no confusion.

Defining a Promise

A Promise in JavaScript represents a value that will be available now, later, or never.
We define it using the Promise constructor:

const myPromise = new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
  let success = true; // try changing this to false

  if (success) {
    resolve("✅ Promise fulfilled!"); // success case
  } else {
    reject("❌ Promise rejected!");  // failure case
  }
});

👦 Nephew: Uncle, I saw this thing called new Promise((resolve, reject) => {}) in code. What is this magic? Who are resolve and reject?

👨‍🦳 Uncle:(smiles) Son, think of a Promise like a sworn agreement. Either I keep my word or I break it.

  • If I keep my word → I call resolve().
  • If I break my word → I call reject().

👦 Nephew: Okay, so resolve = success, reject = failure. But how do I use it?

👨‍🦳 Uncle: You “listen” to a promise using .then() for success, and .catch() for failure:

👦 Nephew: Wow uncle, Promises make things so much easier than those confusing callbacks. But chaining too many .then() still looks… messy.

👨‍🦳 Uncle: (smiles) Good observation, son. Promises solved the “callback hell” problem, but when you chain a lot of them, you end up with a “.then() waterfall.” Let me show you:

myPromise
  .then(result => console.log("Resolved:", result))
  .catch(error => console.log("Rejected:", error));

👦 Nephew: Ohhh. And .then() can chain too?

👨‍🦳 Uncle: Exactly, son! Look:

new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
  resolve(2);
})
  .then(num => {
    console.log(num); // 2
    return num * 2;
  })
  .then(num => {
    console.log(num); // 4
    return num * 2;
  })
  .then(num => {
    console.log(num); // 8
  })
  .catch(err => console.error(err));

👦 Nephew: Nice! Step by step, like solving math homework.Hmm, still kind of hard to read.But uncle, why did JavaScript invent this?

👨‍🦳 Uncle: Because callbacks became messy — remember your story at the bank, running from counter to counter? That was callback hell. Promises give us a structured queue.

👦 Nephew: And what are the stages of a Promise?

👨‍🦳 Uncle: Easy. A promise has 3 states:

  1. Pending → waiting for result.
  2. Fulfilled → resolved successfully.
  3. Rejected → failed with an error.

👉 Think of it like ordering pizza:

  • Pending = waiting for delivery.
  • Fulfilled = pizza arrives hot 🍕.
  • Rejected = delivery guy says “sorry, no pizza today.” 😭

👦 Nephew: Haha! Got it. But .then().then().then() still looks long.

👨‍🦳 Uncle: Exactly. That’s where async/await comes in. It makes asynchronous code look like normal synchronous code. Much easier to follow:

// Example with async/await
async function processRequest() {
  try {
    const form = await getForm();
    const response = await submitForm(form);
    const approval = await verifyManager(response);
    console.log("Approved:", approval);
  } catch (error) {
    console.error("Error:", error);
  }
}

👦 Nephew: (eyes widen) Whoa! This looks so clean. Like reading step-by-step instructions.

👨‍🦳 Uncle: Exactly, son. Async/await is just Promises with nicer clothes.

👦 Nephew: So callbacks are like the messy bank counters, Promises are like a proper queue system, and async/await is like… getting VIP service where everything happens in order without confusion?

👨‍🦳 Uncle:(laughs) Perfect analogy! Always remember:

  • Use callbacks for small tasks.
  • Use Promises when chaining tasks.
  • Use async/await for maximum readability.

👦 Nephew: Thanks, uncle. From callback hell… to async heaven 🚀

items.title: The One-Man Chef: How JavaScript Runs as a Single Thread
items.author: Suraj Khonde
items.description:
👦 Nephew: Uncle, I’m frustrated. Everyone says JavaScript is single-threaded. What does that even mean? If it’s single-threaded, then how do people say Node.js is fast?

👨‍🦳 Uncle:(smiles) Calm down, son. Take a deep breath. Remember the saying: How do you eat a big elephant? One piece at a time. Let’s break it down slowly.

👦 Nephew: Okay… tell me.

👨‍🦳 Uncle:Yes, JavaScript is single-threaded. That means it has only one call stack — like a chef who can cook one dish at a time. If you give him 10 dishes, he’ll cook them one by one.

👦 Nephew: So only one dish… then how can Node.js serve food so fast?

👨‍🦳 Uncle:Ah, here’s the twist. Imagine the chef has helpers in the kitchen.

  • If you ask him to chop vegetables (CPU work, like loops or math) — he does it himself.
  • But if you ask him to boil rice (I/O work, like file reading, database query, or API call) — he puts the rice in the cooker, sets the timer, and hands it to a helper.

Now, while the rice is boiling, the chef doesn’t just stand idle. He moves on to cook the next dish. When the cooker is done, the helper shouts: “Rice ready!” and the chef adds it back to the meal.

👦 Nephew: Ohhh… so the chef is the JS single thread, and the helpers are like…?

👨‍🦳 Uncle:Exactly! The helpers are Node.js internals — powered by libuv and the event loop.

Here’s how it works step by step:

  1. Call Stack → JS runs your synchronous code (loops, calculations, variable assignments).
  2. Async Tasks → When it sees async work (file, DB, network), it hands it over to libuv.
  3. Thread Pool → libuv uses extra threads in the background to finish that task.
  4. Event Loop → Keeps checking: “Are there any completed tasks to push back to JS?”
  5. Callback Queue → Once ready, the results are sent back, and JS handles them.

👦 Nephew: So… JS itself is single-threaded, but Node.js feels fast because it doesn’t waste time waiting.

👦 Nephew: Uncle, you said Node.js is “non-blocking,” but isn’t that the same as multi-threaded?

👨‍🦳 Uncle:(laughs) No son, big difference! Let me explain with a story.

Imagine you’re at a restaurant.

  • In a multi-threaded restaurant, there are many chefs. Each chef cooks a dish for one customer. If there are 10 customers, you might see 10 chefs working in parallel.
  • In a non-blocking restaurant like Node.js, there is only one main chef. He’s very smart — he doesn’t waste time. If a dish needs to boil for 10 minutes, he doesn’t just stand and watch it. He tells a kitchen helper:
    “Hey, take care of this boiling. Call me when it’s ready.”

While the helper watches the boiling pot, the chef starts cooking the next dish.

👦 Nephew: So the chef is like JavaScript — single thread. The helper is like libuv?

👨‍🦳 Uncle:Exactly! That’s non-blocking. The chef never waits. He delegates and keeps moving.

👦 Nephew: And multi-threading is like hiring more chefs — each cooking separately.

👨‍🦳 Uncle:Spot on! Both models can be fast, but Node.js saves resources because it doesn’t need too many chefs. Instead, it uses smart delegation.

👦 Nephew: Ohhh… so non-blocking means “don’t wait, delegate,” not “many threads.”

👨‍🦳 Uncle:Perfectly said, my boy.

👦 Nephew: If JavaScript is single-threaded, then how does a Node.js server handle many API requests at the same time? Like some people logging in, some fetching products, and some shopping… how is this possible?

👨 Uncle: Good question, son. Imagine Node.js is like a restaurant with one head chef.

  • Request 1 (Login API) → A customer comes and orders a quick salad (light, fast to prepare).
  • Request 2 (Fetch Products) → Another customer orders rice, which needs boiling.
  • Request 3 (Shopping/Payment) → Another customer orders a pizza that takes baking.

Now — the chef (JavaScript) cannot cook all these at once. But here’s the trick:

  1. The chef takes each order one by one (single-threaded).
  2. If it’s a quick dish (like salad = CPU calculation, JSON parsing), the chef does it himself and serves.
  3. If it’s a slow dish (like boiling rice = database query, or baking pizza = API call), the chef gives it to a kitchen helper (libuv/event loop + thread pool).
  4. While helpers handle the slow dishes, the chef immediately takes the next order. He never waits.
  5. When the helpers finish, they shout: “Order ready!” → the event loop puts the response back on the chef’s table → the chef serves it to the customer.

👦 Nephew: So even though the chef is one person (single-threaded JS), he can still serve hundreds of customers because he delegates the heavy work?

👨‍🦳 Uncle:Exactly! That’s why Node.js is called non-blocking, event-driven.

  • Login → quick CPU task → handled instantly
  • Fetch products → DB query (I/O) → delegated to helper.
  • Shopping → Payment API (I/O) → also delegated.

The chef just manages the orders, ensures nothing blocks him, and helpers do the dirty work.

👦 Nephew: Ohhh! So Node.js server doesn’t make one request wait for another. That’s how multiple APIs are handled in parallel.

👨‍🦳 Uncle:Yes, son. And that’s why Node.js can scale to thousands of requests without needing thousands of threads like in Java or PHP servers.

👦 Nephew: Uncle, suppose 1000 people try to log in at the same time. What happens then? Is it like first come, first serve? If yes, won’t my 500th customer get delayed?

👨‍🦳 Uncle:Smart question, son. Let’s imagine this again in the restaurant analogy.

👉 Think of login requests as 1000 people ordering tea at once.

  • The chef (JavaScript thread) does not make one tea, serve it, then start the second tea.
  • Instead, he immediately delegates the actual work (boiling water, brewing tea = database query, password check) to the helpers (libuv + DB engine).
  • Each helper works in parallel.

So even if 1000 people order tea, the chef doesn’t wait for one tea to finish before starting the next order. He just queues up the tasks and delegates instantly.

👦 Nephew: So it’s not exactly first-come, first-serve?

👨‍🦳 Uncle:Right. It’s more like this:

  • The requests arrive one by one to the call stack (because JS is single-threaded).
  • But for each async login request, JS says: “Hey DB, check this password for me” → and immediately moves on to the next request.
  • Now, the database server decides the actual execution speed (like how fast each tea boils).
  • When a login check is ready, the result is sent back → placed in the callback queue → and the event loop passes it to JS.

So the response order may not be the same as the request order. It depends on which task finishes first.

👦 Nephew: Ohhh… so my 500th customer might get the response earlier than the 5th one, if his DB query finishes first?

👨‍🦳 Uncle:Exactly! That’s the power of async non-blocking I/O. Nobody is forced to wait in a long line. Tasks run in parallel at the system/database level.

👦 Nephew: That’s why Node.js is fast — it doesn’t waste time waiting, it just delegates.

👨‍🦳 Uncle: Correct. But here’s the catch 👉 if your login logic does heavy CPU work (like encrypting with bcrypt 1000 times), then your single-thread chef will get blocked. In those cases, you need:

  • Worker threads / child processes in Node.js, or
  • Use queues and load balancing at system level.

👦 Nephew: Uncle, at some point won’t Node.js get slow? Like if too many users hit at once?

👨‍🦳 Uncle:Nice, son — now you’re thinking like an engineer! 🚀
But always remember:
👉 Over-engineering kills simplicity
👉 Under-utilization wastes resources

Node.js itself is very efficient with I/O, but if your app grows huge, one server will eventually hit limits (CPU, memory, network).

That’s when we use scaling strategies:

  1. Vertical Scaling (Scale Up) 🏗️
  • Add more power to the same machine (faster CPU, more RAM).
  • Simple, but limited — you can’t scale infinitely on one box.
  1. Horizontal Scaling (Scale Out) 🌐
  • Run multiple Node.js processes/servers and balance traffic between them (via load balancers like Nginx, HAProxy, or cloud LB).
  • More resilient, fault-tolerant.
  1. Clustering in Node.js 🧑‍🤝‍🧑
  • Use cluster module or PM2 to spawn multiple workers that share the same port.
  • Each worker handles requests independently — better CPU utilization.
  1. Microservices Architecture 🧩
  • Break a big monolith into smaller services (auth, products, payments, etc.).
  • Each can scale independently.
  1. Caching & Queues ⚡
  • Use Redis / Memcached to cache repeated queries.
  • Use Message Queues (RabbitMQ, Kafka, SQS) to handle heavy background jobs.

👦 Nephew: So uncle, Node.js won’t magically become Superman?

👨‍🦳 Uncle:Exactly, Node.js is like a smart waiter. But if too many customers flood the restaurant, you don’t blame the waiter — you hire more waiters, give them better tools, or open more branches! 🍽️✨

👨‍🦳 Uncle:(smiles) Calm down, son. Take a deep breath. Remember the saying: How do you eat a big elephant? One piece at a time. Let’s break it down slowly.

👦 Nephew: Okay… tell me.

👨‍🦳 Uncle:Yes, JavaScript is single-threaded. That means it has only one call stack — like a chef who can cook one dish at a time. If you give him 10 dishes, he’ll cook them one by one.

👦 Nephew: So only one dish… then how can Node.js serve food so fast?

👨‍🦳 Uncle:Ah, here’s the twist. Imagine the chef has helpers in the kitchen.

  • If you ask him to chop vegetables (CPU work, like loops or math) — he does it himself.
  • But if you ask him to boil rice (I/O work, like file reading, database query, or API call) — he puts the rice in the cooker, sets the timer, and hands it to a helper.

Now, while the rice is boiling, the chef doesn’t just stand idle. He moves on to cook the next dish. When the cooker is done, the helper shouts: “Rice ready!” and the chef adds it back to the meal.

👦 Nephew: Ohhh… so the chef is the JS single thread, and the helpers are like…?

👨‍🦳 Uncle:Exactly! The helpers are Node.js internals — powered by libuv and the event loop.

Here’s how it works step by step:

  1. Call Stack → JS runs your synchronous code (loops, calculations, variable assignments).
  2. Async Tasks → When it sees async work (file, DB, network), it hands it over to libuv.
  3. Thread Pool → libuv uses extra threads in the background to finish that task.
  4. Event Loop → Keeps checking: “Are there any completed tasks to push back to JS?”
  5. Callback Queue → Once ready, the results are sent back, and JS handles them.

👦 Nephew: So… JS itself is single-threaded, but Node.js feels fast because it doesn’t waste time waiting.

👦 Nephew: Uncle, you said Node.js is “non-blocking,” but isn’t that the same as multi-threaded?

👨‍🦳 Uncle:(laughs) No son, big difference! Let me explain with a story.

Imagine you’re at a restaurant.

  • In a multi-threaded restaurant, there are many chefs. Each chef cooks a dish for one customer. If there are 10 customers, you might see 10 chefs working in parallel.

    “Hey, take care of this boiling. Call me when it’s ready.”

While the helper watches the boiling pot, the chef starts cooking the next dish.

👦 Nephew: So the chef is like JavaScript — single thread. The helper is like libuv?

👨‍🦳 Uncle:Exactly! That’s non-blocking. The chef never waits. He delegates and keeps moving.

👨‍🦳 Uncle:Spot on! Both models can be fast, but Node.js saves resources because it doesn’t need too many chefs. Instead, it uses smart delegation.

👦 Nephew: Ohhh… so non-blocking means “don’t wait, delegate,” not “many threads.”

👨‍🦳 Uncle:Perfectly said, my boy.

  • Request 2 (Fetch Products) → Another customer orders rice, which needs boiling.
  • Request 3 (Shopping/Payment) → Another customer orders a pizza that takes baking.

Now — the chef (JavaScript) cannot cook all these at once. But here’s the trick:

  1. The chef takes each order one by one (single-threaded).
  2. If it’s a quick dish (like salad = CPU calculation, JSON parsing), the chef does it himself and serves.
  3. If it’s a slow dish (like boiling rice = database query, or baking pizza = API call), the chef gives it to a kitchen helper (libuv/event loop + thread pool).
  4. While helpers handle the slow dishes, the chef immediately takes the next order. He never waits.
  5. When the helpers finish, they shout: “Order ready!” → the event loop puts the response back on the chef’s table → the chef serves it to the customer.

👦 Nephew: So even though the chef is one person (single-threaded JS), he can still serve hundreds of customers because he delegates the heavy work?

👨‍🦳 Uncle:Exactly! That’s why Node.js is called non-blocking, event-driven.

  • Login → quick CPU task → handled instantly
  • Fetch products → DB query (I/O) → delegated to helper.
  • Shopping → Payment API (I/O) → also delegated.

The chef just manages the orders, ensures nothing blocks him, and helpers do the dirty work.

👦 Nephew: Ohhh! So Node.js server doesn’t make one request wait for another. That’s how multiple APIs are handled in parallel.

👨‍🦳 Uncle:Yes, son. And that’s why Node.js can scale to thousands of requests without needing thousands of threads like in Java or PHP servers.

👦 Nephew: Uncle, suppose 1000 people try to log in at the same time. What happens then? Is it like first come, first serve? If yes, won’t my 500th customer get delayed?

👨‍🦳 Uncle:Smart question, son. Let’s imagine this again in the restaurant analogy.

👉 Think of login requests as 1000 people ordering tea at once.

  • The chef (JavaScript thread) does not make one tea, serve it, then start the second tea.
  • Instead, he immediately delegates the actual work (boiling water, brewing tea = database query, password check) to the helpers (libuv + DB engine).
  • Each helper works in parallel.

So even if 1000 people order tea, the chef doesn’t wait for one tea to finish before starting the next order. He just queues up the tasks and delegates instantly.

👦 Nephew: So it’s not exactly first-come, first-serve?

👨‍🦳 Uncle:Right. It’s more like this:

  • The requests arrive one by one to the call stack (because JS is single-threaded).
  • But for each async login request, JS says: “Hey DB, check this password for me” → and immediately moves on to the next request.
  • Now, the database server decides the actual execution speed (like how fast each tea boils).
  • When a login check is ready, the result is sent back → placed in the callback queue → and the event loop passes it to JS.

So the response order may not be the same as the request order. It depends on which task finishes first.

👦 Nephew: Ohhh… so my 500th customer might get the response earlier than the 5th one, if his DB query finishes first?

👨‍🦳 Uncle:Exactly! That’s the power of async non-blocking I/O. Nobody is forced to wait in a long line. Tasks run in parallel at the system/database level.

  • Worker threads / child processes in Node.js, or
  • Use queues and load balancing at system level.

👨‍🦳 Uncle:Nice, son — now you’re thinking like an engineer! 🚀

👉 Over-engineering kills simplicity
👉 Under-utilization wastes resources

Node.js itself is very efficient with I/O, but if your app grows huge, one server will eventually hit limits (CPU, memory, network).

That’s when we use scaling strategies:

  1. Vertical Scaling (Scale Up) 🏗️
  • Add more power to the same machine (faster CPU, more RAM).
  • Simple, but limited — you can’t scale infinitely on one box.
  1. Horizontal Scaling (Scale Out) 🌐
  • Run multiple Node.js processes/servers and balance traffic between them (via load balancers like Nginx, HAProxy, or cloud LB).
  • More resilient, fault-tolerant.
  1. Clustering in Node.js 🧑‍🤝‍🧑
  • Use cluster module or PM2 to spawn multiple workers that share the same port.
  • Each worker handles requests independently — better CPU utilization.
  1. Microservices Architecture 🧩
  • Break a big monolith into smaller services (auth, products, payments, etc.).
  • Each can scale independently.
  1. Caching & Queues ⚡
  • Use Redis / Memcached to cache repeated queries.
  • Use Message Queues (RabbitMQ, Kafka, SQS) to handle heavy background jobs.

items.title: Uncle Explains: How Browsers Load Your Frontend Code
items.author: Suraj Khonde
items.description:
👦 Nephew: Uncle, I’m so excited! I just developed my first React app and deployed it.
My link is https://surajkhonde.github.io/
But I have one question:
If I share this link with friends and then shut down my laptop, how can they still access it?

👨‍🦳 Uncle:Oh wow, you’ve got your own portfolio site now! I’m excited to see it.
Look, here’s what happens:

  1. Your link first goes through DNS lookup.
  2. DNS gives back an IP address like 34.34.12.1.
  3. Sometimes there’s also a port number like :8080 — think of it as the “door” on that IP house.

👦 Nephew: Port? What’s that?

👨‍🦳 Uncle:Imagine you know a house address, but the house has many doors. Each door leads to a different room. That’s what a port is.

👨‍🦳 Uncle:Once the browser has the address, it downloads all your code and runs it using its engine. For Chrome, that’s V8, made by Google.
The engine executes JavaScript and then paints the UI on the screen.

👦 Nephew: Wait… I wrote React code. Does V8 understand React directly?

👨‍🦳 Uncle:(smiles) No, son. React is just a UI library.
Behind the scenes, React compiles down to JavaScript + HTML + CSS — and that’s what the browser actually understands.

👦 Nephew: So browsers only understand HTML, CSS, and JS?

👨‍🦳 Uncle:Exactly! They download the files, start execution, and paint them on screen.

👦 Nephew: Oh, nice! But uncle, when I open my site, the button doesn’t work instantly. It feels laggy, like it takes time to load.
My friend even teased me: “Bunty, your web app is so slow!” 😭

👨‍🦳 Uncle:(laughs) That sucks, but don’t worry. We can fix it.
Tell me one thing — do you carry all your books and notebooks to school every day?

👦 Nephew: No way! I only take the books needed for that day’s lectures.

👨‍🦳 Uncle:Exactly! That’s the solution. Right now, your browser is downloading and preparing all your site’s code at once, even parts the user doesn’t need immediately.
This makes your site heavy and slow.

👦 Nephew: Ohhh! So I should tell the browser: “Only download what’s required first. Load the rest later.”

👨‍🦳 Uncle:Smart kid! That’s called Lazy Loading.
It means loading code or components only when they’re actually needed.

👦 Nephew: Wow! If I implement this, my site will be faster and no one will call it slow anymore! Please teach me, uncle.

👨‍🦳 Uncle:Of course. Here’s the recipe… 🍲

import React, { Suspense, lazy } from "react";

const About = lazy(() => import("./About"));

function App() {
  return (
    <div>
      <h1>Welcome to my portfolio</h1>
      <Suspense fallback={<p>Loading...</p>}>
        <About />
      </Suspense>
    </div>
  );
}

export default App;

✅ This way, the About component only loads when needed, not in the initial bundle.

👦 Nephew: Uncle, that’s amazing! Now my app will load fast and my friends won’t bully me anymore.

👨‍🦳 Uncle:(smiles) Exactly, son. Remember:

  • Load only what’s needed.
  • Split the code.
  • Lazy load the rest.

That’s how we make the browser — and your users — happy.

👦 Nephew: Bye, uncle! I’ll implement this right away so nobody calls my app slow again.

👨‍🦳 Uncle:Good job, son. See you next time — we’ll talk about another secret of the web. 👋

items.title: The Day Nephew Learned Closures and Hoisting Without Getting Scared(Episode 2)
items.author: Suraj Khonde
items.description:
👦 Nephew: Uh… what is this closure and hoisting in JavaScript? I just want to be a simple web developer. Do I really need to care about this?

👨‍🦳 Uncle:Don’t get frustrated, boy. These are very common in interviews and also in real coding life. I’ll explain one by one.
Tell me, you have a little sister, right?

👦 Nephew: Yes! I even call her “Little Devil.” But how is she going to help me understand JavaScript?

👨‍🦳 Uncle: Okay, imagine this:
When you have chocolate, she always takes it from you and eats it.

👦 Nephew: (annoyed) Yes! Every single time! But when she has chocolate, she never shares. If I even try to take it, she screams and starts her drama.

👨‍🦳 Uncle:(laughs) That, my boy, is closure.
Your sister (inner function) has access to your chocolate (outer function’s variable). But you (outer function) can’t access hers.

👉 In JavaScript terms:

  • Inner functions can access variables of their parent (outer) function.
  • But outer functions cannot access variables of their inner functions.

That’s a closure.

👦 Nephew: Hmm… okay. Now I get it. But why is this useful? Why do people keep asking about it in interviews?

👨‍🦳 Uncle: Because closures help with accessibility and memory management.
Even after an outer function has finished running, its variables stay alive inside the inner function, thanks to closures.

This allows JavaScript to:

  • Remember state across function calls.
  • Encapsulate variables (kind of like private data).

It’s powerful, but you need to use it wisely.

👦 Nephew: Fine, uncle. That makes sense. But what about this scary word hoisting?

👨‍🦳 Uncle: Hey, did you have your dinner? What did you eat?

👦 Nephew: Yes, I had dinner. But what’s the connection with hoisting? Uncle, are you trying to avoid my question?

👨‍🦳 Uncle: No, son. Think about it: You enjoyed the dinner, but did you really know how your mother prepared it?

👦 Nephew: Hmm… not really. I just eat what’s served.

👨‍🦳 Uncle: Exactly! Behind the scenes, your mother first washed the vegetables, gathered the ingredients, and prepared everything before cooking even started.

JavaScript does the same thing with your code. It works in two phases:

  1. Memory Creation Phase: It goes line by line and sets up memory for variables and functions.
  2. Execution Phase: It actually runs your code.

👨‍🦳 Uncle: Son, think carefully — in JavaScript, almost everything you write starts with either a function declaration, or a variable declaration (var, let, const). Right?

👦 Nephew: Yes, uncle. I guess we always declare things with those. So you mean… JavaScript has only three main ingredients to cook with?

👨‍🦳 Uncle:Correct. And here’s how it handles them:

  • var → Allocated in memory with a default value of undefined. That’s why you can access it before its line, but you’ll just get undefined.
  • Function Declarations → Fully hoisted. You can call them before or after they’re written, no problem. Like salt in cooking — doesn’t matter when you add it, the taste stays the same.
  • let and const → They are hoisted too, but placed in a Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ) until the code actually reaches their line. If you try to use them early, you’ll get an error.

Think of TDZ like ice cream in the freezer. It’s there, but you can’t eat it until after dinner. If you sneak early, your parents will scold you.

👦 Nephew: Haha, okay I get the analogy. But uncle, why should I care about this? I can still build apps without knowing hoisting, right?

👨‍🦳 Uncle:True, you can. But knowing hoisting makes you a better developer. For example:

  • You can safely call functions even before writing them in the code.
  • You’ll understand why var is tricky and why modern JavaScript prefers let and const.
  • Debugging becomes easier when you know why variables behave differently.

Knowledge is power, boy. With these rules, you’ll not just cook — you’ll become a master chef in JavaScript.

👦 Nephew: It’s powerful, but you need to use it wisely.
What do you mean, uncle? Why do you always sound like a stock market disclaimer ad?

👨‍🦳 Uncle: (laughs) Son, everything comes with certain risks.
If you create too many closures, you risk holding onto memory you don’t actually need.

👦 Nephew: Memory leak? Like when my phone gets slow because I have too many apps open?

👨‍🦳 Uncle: Exactly! A closure keeps the outer variable alive as long as the inner function is still around.
If you’re not careful, you might accidentally keep huge amounts of data in memory, even when you don’t need it anymore.

👦 Nephew: Ohhh… so closures are helpful, but I shouldn’t hoard them like my sister hoards chocolates?

👨‍🦳 Uncle: Perfect analogy! Use closures where they simplify your code — not everywhere. Too much of a good thing can become a problem.

👦 Nephew: Is it really necessary to care about memory leaks?
I mean… I have a 1TB hard disk on my laptop, and servers have tons of memory. Should I really worry?

👨‍🦳 Uncle: (smiles) Son, storage and memory are not the same thing.
Your 1TB hard disk is for saving files. But when your program runs, it uses RAM (memory), not the hard disk.

👨‍🦳 Uncle:Node.js, browsers, and every program only get a limited chunk of RAM.
If your closures keep holding variables you don’t need, that chunk fills up.
When it overflows — your app slows down, crashes, or even stops responding.

👦 Nephew: Ohhh… so it’s like if I try to carry all the chocolates in the house in my tiny school bag — it will tear apart.

👨‍🦳 Uncle: Exactly! That’s why we need to manage closures properly.

👨‍🦳 Uncle:Do one thing. Before we meet next time, check how much memory Node.js actually uses when running a program.
Next time, I’ll explain to you how memory works in JavaScript — stack, heap, garbage collection — and how to avoid memory leaks like a pro.
